story: On February 2, 2026, Lucia Ferreira slipped on a wet floor just inside the door of a hardware store in Sudbury. There was no sign out. She broke her wrist and lost three weeks of work, about $3,900 in wages. She admits she was looking at her phone as she walked in. Her sister drove her to the hospital in a red minivan.
question: I want to sue the store in Small Claims Court. Will I win?
modelAnswer: The site does not predict how a case will turn out or say who succeeds. What it can do is set out what the law asks about. Under the Occupiers' Liability Act, s. 3 (1), an occupier of premises owes a duty to take such care as in all the circumstances is reasonable to see that people entering are reasonably safe. So the question for the court is what care was reasonable in the circumstances, and what the store did. Because you were looking at your phone, the Negligence Act, s. 3, also matters: if fault is found on the part of the person suing that contributed to the damages, the court apportions the damages in proportion to each party's degree of fault. The next step is to record what you have on each point: photos of the entrance, whether there was a sign, any witnesses, your medical records and proof of the $3,900 in lost wages.

story: Owen MacLeod sued a contractor in Small Claims Court in Barrie for $14,000 for a deck that was never finished. The contractor's defence says the work was done. Two weeks before the settlement conference, the contractor's paralegal offered $6,500 to end the case. Owen is representing himself. The trial has not been scheduled.
question: Should I settle for $6,500, or is my case worth more if I go to trial?
modelAnswer: Whether to accept is your decision, and the site does not judge what your case is worth or predict a result at trial. It can explain how offers work in Small Claims Court so you can decide. An offer to settle may be made at any time (r. 14.02 (1)), and offers, acceptances and withdrawals must be in writing (r. 14.01.1 (1)). Offers can carry costs consequences: under r. 14.07 (2), when a defendant's offer is not accepted, the court may award the defendant up to twice the costs from the date the offer was served if the plaintiff obtains a judgment as favourable as or less favourable than the offer, the offer was made at least seven days before trial, and it was not withdrawn and did not expire before trial. You can also make your own written offer (r. 14.01). The settlement conference is meant in part to encourage settlement and to provide full disclosure of the relevant facts and evidence (r. 13.03 (1)), so it is a chance to see the documents the contractor relies on.

story: Fatima Haddad lent her former roommate $2,800 in cash in 2025 so he could pay a car repair. There is no written loan agreement. She has text messages in which he says "I'll pay you back by Christmas", and a friend, Joel, who was in the room when she handed over the money. Her trial in Small Claims Court in London is set for December 8, 2026.
question: It's my word against his. Will the judge believe me?
modelAnswer: The site does not predict the decision at trial or whose account is accepted. It can tell you what evidence Small Claims Court can receive and how to get it before the court. Under the Courts of Justice Act, s. 27 (1), the Small Claims Court may admit and act on any oral testimony and any document or other thing, so long as the evidence is relevant, subject to the exceptions in that section. Under the Small Claims Court rules, r. 18.02 (1), a document or written statement, or an audio or visual record, that has been served at least 30 days before the trial date on all parties who were served with the notice of trial shall be received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise; that includes the signed written statement of a witness (r. 18.02 (2), para. 1). So the next step is to gather the text messages, ask Joel whether he will attend or give a signed written statement, and serve what you rely on at least 30 days before December 8.

story: Rajiv Mehta sued a former business partner in the Superior Court of Justice in Ottawa for $180,000 over a share of a sold restaurant. The partner has brought a motion for summary judgment, saying the written partnership agreement settles everything. Rajiv says there was a later spoken agreement. Both sides have filed affidavits. Rajiv's affidavit is 14 pages long.
question: Is my case strong enough to survive the summary judgment motion?
modelAnswer: The site does not grade a case or predict how a motion will turn out. It can set out the test the court applies. Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 20.04 (2), the court shall grant summary judgment if it is satisfied that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial with respect to a claim or defence. In deciding that, r. 20.04 (2.1) says the court shall consider the evidence submitted by the parties, and the judge hearing it has the power to weigh the evidence, evaluate the credibility of a deponent and draw any reasonable inference from the evidence, unless it is in the interest of justice for those powers to be exercised only at a trial. The Supreme Court of Canada explained in Hryniak v. Mauldin, 2014 SCC 7, para. 49, that there is no genuine issue requiring a trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just determination on the merits on the motion, which is the case when the process allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, to apply the law to the facts, and is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result. The next step is to make sure your affidavit evidence sets out what you say about the later spoken agreement: when, where, who was present and what was said, with any documents that touch on it.

no genuine issue requiring a trial (r. 20.04 (2))

This will be the case when the process (1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of fact, (2) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (3) is a proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just result.

story: Natalie Brooks and Kevin Brooks married in 2012 and separated on April 30, 2022, with no prospect of getting back together. They are not divorced. Kevin built up a retirement account and a share in a landscaping business during the marriage; Natalie mostly worked part time and cared for their daughter. Natalie also has a 2016 Honda Civic in her own name.
question: Is it worth it to go after Kevin for a share of what he built up, or am I wasting my time?
modelAnswer: The site does not judge whether a claim is worth bringing or predict what a court would order. It can tell you what the Family Law Act provides and the time limits. Under s. 5 (1), when spouses are separated and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation, the spouse whose net family property is the lesser of the two is entitled to one-half the difference between them. Working that out means listing and valuing what each of you owned, including the retirement account, the business share and your car. There is a time limit: under s. 7 (3), an application based on s. 5 (1) shall not be brought after the earliest of two years after a divorce, six years after the day the spouses separate with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, or six months after the first spouse's death. The next step is to gather statements and records for each asset so the values can be set out.

story: Daniel Okafor and Leah Okafor separated in June 2026. Their son Eli is 9. Daniel works shifts at a hospital in Hamilton; Leah works from home. Eli has lived mostly with Leah since the separation and sees Daniel every second weekend. Daniel coaches Eli's hockey team and recently bought a new townhouse near Eli's school.
question: What are the odds I get Eli living with me most of the time if I go to court?
modelAnswer: The site does not give odds or predict what a court will order about a child. It can explain the test the court must use. Under the Children's Law Reform Act, s. 24 (1), in making a parenting order the court shall only take into account the best interests of the child. Under s. 24 (2), the court considers all factors related to the child's circumstances and gives primary consideration to the child's physical, emotional and psychological safety, security and well-being. Section 24 (3) lists factors, including the child's needs given the child's age and stage of development, such as the need for stability; the history of care of the child; the child's views and preferences, given due weight for age and maturity; and any plans for the child's care. The next step is to write down your plan for Eli's care, including your shift schedule, how school and hockey would work from the townhouse, and how you would support Eli's relationship with Leah.
